newsitem.title: USA: U.N. envoy sees Mobutu return boosting peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy sees Mobutu return boosting peace hopes.

text.p: The U.N. special envoy to Central Africa said on Monday he believed Tuesday's return home by Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko would speed diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis in the region.

"The fact that Mobutu is (going) back now for me is an indication that you will see some action, hopefully diplomatic," Canadian ambassador to the United States Raymond Chretien said in an interview with Reuters.

Chretien, who recently returned from a month-long tour of the region, suggested in a report to the United Nations last week that it appoint a special representative to the area racked by ethnic conflicts.

Mobutu, 66, will fly home from France after a four-month absence for cancer treatment during which Tutsi rebels have taken over a swath of territory in the east of the country, routing the demoralised and ill-disciplined Zairean army.
"I think that his return will result in a lot of loose threads being picked up by him," Chretien said.
"I would certainly hope that he would go for a negotiated solution," he said, both internally with the rebels and externally in his relationship with Rwanda.

Chretien said that in two meetings he held with Mobutu in France, the Zairean president had made clear he favoured negotiation to recover lost territory, although some Mobutu advisers took a tougher line, branding the rebels as traitors.

With the majority of an estimated 1.2 million Rwandan refugees in Zaire and Tanzania apparently having returned home or being now on their way, plans for a Canadian-led multinational force to go to the region have been shelved.
Chretien said he believed that for "the first time in history" the mere threat of sending such a force had helped to ease the situation.
But he said that despite the return of the bulk of the refugees, "the big problems are still there."

These included how to assimilate the refugees, most of them ethnic Hutus, back into a Rwanda now ruled by a Tutsi-led government, continuing conflict in Burundi, the hostility between Zaire and Rwanda and the whole future of Zaire.
"There is work for years and years," Chretien said.

He said the U.N. representative he was suggesting "could certainly dampen this kind of sabre-rattling that is heard in Kinshasa, try to convince the government in Zaire that they should get through negotiation what they want to get back."

In his report, Chretien offered three options for the special representative: one resident in the region; a roving official who would tour the region for several months; or one who would visit the region when needed.
The envoy said he believed opinion at the United Nations supported his preference for a resident representative, provided practical problems including funding could be resolved.
He said both outgoing U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt and his newly chosen successor Kofi Annan of Ghana were "very much aware of the situation."
"I'm sure they will agree with my recommendations, the question is when they implement them," he said.
Chretien said he was not a candidate for the post, saying his job as ambassador to Washington was too important.
